objectives: Write a clear search and narrow it with one filter.
Judge whether a source fits your question, and record where you found it.
Fill in an online form with only what is needed, and read the confirmation.
Save a file with a clear name in a folder you can find, and pack it in a ZIP file.
Choose who can view, comment or edit, and pick the right way to get a file back.
outcomes: Search: in Microsoft Edge at a lab workstation, given a local service need, each learner writes a search that names the service, the provider and the place, then applies one refinement (quotation marks, site: or a date range) and says in one sentence what it changed. Correct with no more than one prompt, and no plus signs.

Sources: for one result from that search, each learner records the five source fields (title, organization, web address, date checked and the detail used), answers the five source questions from slide 5, and names one detail to confirm with the organization that runs the service. All five fields are present and each judgment points to something on the page.

Forms: using the practice form on slide 10 with fictional details, each learner submits once with a required choice missing, reads the message, completes the form, and explains that the confirmation does not mean anyone received a request.

Files: in File Explorer at a lab workstation, each learner makes a folder named Community resources, saves a Word file in it as library-help-v1.docx, reopens it from that folder, compresses the folder to a ZIP file, extracts it and opens the extracted copy. All steps done, with nothing saved in the wrong place.

Access and recovery: using the permission practice on slide 15 (simulated), each learner chooses Viewer, Commenter or Editor for a reader, a reviewer and a co-writer, giving each the least access the task needs; restores a deleted practice file from the Recycle Bin; says when version history is the right tool instead; and says that read-only stops changes but is not encryption. All correct with no more than one prompt.

Slides 21, 22 and 23. Home task: search for one service you need, write the five-field source note, and keep it in a named folder on your own device or on paper; share it at the start of week 3. lab: Write a question about a local public service you or a neighbor might need, such as computer help at a public library. Name the service and the town.

In Edge, search for that service and record your search. Then refine it one way: a phrase in quotation marks, site:gov, or Tools › Any time on google.com. Record what changed. Plus signs are not needed.
Open one result that answers your question. Record the page title, the organization, the web address (Ctrl and L, Ctrl and C, then Ctrl and V here), today's date and the one detail you will use.

For that page, answer the five source questions from slide 5 in a few words each: who made it, what evidence it gives, why it was published, whether it is current, and whether it fits your question. Name one detail to confirm with the organization.

On slide 10, select Review practice request with one choice left blank, and write the message you see. Then choose a topic and a contact method, submit, and copy the confirmation. Say what the confirmation does not prove.

Open File Explorer (Windows logo key and E) › Documents. Make a folder named Community resources. In Word, type your task 1 question and task 3 source note, and save the file in that folder as library-help-v1.docx. Close Word, reopen the file from the folder, and say who controls a copy kept in a cloud drive.

On slide 15, choose access for three people: one who only reads, one who suggests wording, and one who writes the handout with you. Record each role and why, and mark it simulated. Say what read-only does and does not do.

Right-click Community resources › Show more options › Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder. Right-click the ZIP file › Extract All, then open the extracted file. Delete that file and restore it from the Recycle Bin. On slide 18, choose the route for wrong wording and mark it simulated.
answers: The question names a service and a town, for example: Where can I get computer help at a public library in [town]?

The first search names the service and place, with no plus signs. One refinement is used (quotation marks, site:gov or a date range) and its effect is stated, such as fewer, more local or more recent results. Ranking is not treated as proof.
All five fields: page title, organization, full web address, date checked and one specific detail. No personal records.

Who made it (credibility), what evidence it gives (accuracy), why it was published (perspective and bias), whether it is current, and whether it fits the question (relevance), each tied to something on the page. One detail, such as hours or eligibility, to confirm through the organization's own contact.
Message: Please select an item in the list. Confirmation: Practice complete … No request was sent. It shows the exercise was done, not that anyone received a request.

Documents › Community resources holds library-help-v1.docx, reopened from that folder. The service and account (or the organization) control a cloud copy; the person who shares a file stays the owner.

Reader: Viewer. Reviewer: Commenter, or the nearest option the service offers. Co-writer: Editor. Named people and the least access each task needs, marked simulated. Read-only stops changes but the file can still be read and copied; it is not encryption.

The ZIP file holds the folder and the extracted file opens. The deleted file is back in its folder from the Recycle Bin. Wrong wording: version history (simulated; it needs a service such as OneDrive or Google Docs). Missing file: the Recycle Bin or the service's recycle bin. Backup: a separate copy for when every synced copy is gone. A ZIP packages files; it is not encryption or a backup.

slide_changes.title: Write a useful search
slide_changes.body: Include the service, the provider and the place. Try: public library computer help and your town's name. Plus signs are not needed between words. Remove words that distract from the task.

slide_changes.title: Refine without hiding useful results
slide_changes.body: Quotation marks find an exact phrase. site: limits results to one website or kind of website, such as site:gov; it does not prove a page is accurate. A date filter shows recent pages. Each filter can also hide a useful page.

slide_changes.title: Accuracy and relevance differ
slide_changes.body: A correct page about another state's library may not answer a local question. A recent page can still be biased or wrong. A summary or AI answer at the top of the results is not the source; open the organization's own page.

slide_changes.title: Name files so you can find them
slide_changes.body: Use a clear subject and version: library-help-v1.docx. Keep related files in one folder, such as Community resources. Avoid names such as final-final-new.

slide_changes.title: Central storage needs clear access
slide_changes.body: A shared drive keeps one common copy in one place. The service, account or organization controls who can open it and how long it is kept. Sharing a link does not make someone the owner.

slide_changes.title: Sync, backup, and recovery
slide_changes.body: Sync copies changes, including deletions, between your computer and an online service. A backup is a separate copy kept somewhere else. Version history, kept by services such as OneDrive and Google Docs, may bring back earlier wording.

slide_changes.title: Choose who can change the file
slide_changes.body: A viewer reads. A commenter suggests, where the service offers it. An editor changes content. Google Drive says Viewer, Commenter and Editor; OneDrive says Can view and Can edit. Give each named person the least access the task needs.

slide_changes.title: Read-only is not encryption
slide_changes.body: Read-only stops changes, but the file can still be read and copied. Encryption scrambles the content so only someone with the password or key can read it. A password to open and a password to modify protect different things.

slide_changes.title: Compression packages files
slide_changes.body: A ZIP file bundles several files into one and can make them smaller to send. Extract it before editing. Photos and video are often already compressed. A ZIP file is not encryption or a backup.

slide_changes.title: Recover the right thing
slide_changes.body: Missing file? Check the Recycle Bin or the service's recycle bin. Wrong wording? Use version history, which needs a service such as OneDrive or Google Docs. Preview first and tell collaborators before restoring.

slide_changes.title: Knowledge check: a credible page
options: Trust it because it is the top search result
Trust it because several websites repeat it
Confirm it with the organization that runs it
slide_changes.why: Ranking and repetition do not prove a claim. The organization that runs the service is in a position to know, so confirm through its own website or phone number.

slide_changes.title: Lab: build a resource folder
slide_changes.body: Do each worksheet task in its cycle. Save your file in the Community resources folder. Mark sharing and version history as simulated.

prep: Each station: Microsoft Edge, Microsoft Word (Notepad works if Word is missing; save as library-help-v1.txt), File Explorer with a local Documents folder that is not signed in to OneDrive, headphones, and this lesson and worksheet. At the front: the projector showing Edge, File Explorer and Word, and one real West Virginia public library page for the search and source demonstrations, checked the day before. The lab has no cloud account for learners, so sharing (worksheet task 7) and version history (task 8) use the slide 15 and slide 18 practice, marked simulated; if you have your own OneDrive or Google account, you may show the Share box and version history on the projector with a fictional file only. No printing is needed; decide whether learners may print their worksheet or should save it as a PDF before closing. Play video chapters 2, 6 and 7 with captions to check sound, and mark the pause points 1:17, 3:29, 5:02 and 6:35. After your own run-through, delete your practice folder and ZIP from Documents and select Start fresh on this computer at each station. No paid service, real purchase or new learner account is required.
lab_paths: Search from the address bar
Press Ctrl and L, type your words and press Enter. Edge searches with Bing. Plus signs are not needed between words.
Search for an exact phrase
Put the phrase in quotation marks, for example "computer help". Remove the quotation marks if you get too few results.
Search one kind of website
Type site: and the site or ending with no space, then your words, for example site:gov library computer help.
Show only recent results
Go to google.com and search. Below the search box, select Tools, then Any time, and choose a range such as Past year.
Find a word on a long page
Press Ctrl and F, then type the word you want to find on the page.
Copy a web address into your notes
Press Ctrl and L to select the address, then Ctrl and C to copy it. Click in your notes and press Ctrl and V to paste.
Make a new folder
Press the Windows logo key and E to open File Explorer. Open Documents, select New › Folder, type the name and press Enter. Or press Ctrl and Shift and N.
Save a Word file into that folder
In Word, select File › Save As › Browse. Open Documents › Community resources, type the File name, then select Save.
Rename a file
In File Explorer, select the file and press F2, or right-click it and select Rename. Type the new name and press Enter.
Make a ZIP file
Right-click the folder, then select Show more options › Send to › Compressed (zipped) folder. The ZIP file appears next to the folder.
Open the files in a ZIP
Right-click the ZIP file, select Extract All, then follow the steps. Open the files from the new folder, not from inside the ZIP.
Get back a deleted file
Open the Recycle Bin on the desktop, right-click the file and select Restore. It returns to its folder. Shift and Delete skips the Recycle Bin.
Protect a Word file (instructor shows)
File › Info › Protect Document. Always Open Read-Only limits changes; Encrypt with Password asks for a password to open. Word cannot recover a lost password.
Share or see earlier versions (instructor shows; needs an account)

OneDrive: select the file › Share, then choose Can view or Can edit; right-click the file › Version history. Google Drive: Share › Viewer, Commenter or Editor; in a Google Doc, select Last edit at the top right to see versions.
